The Parthenon (; Ancient Greek: Παρθενών, romanised: Parthenōn [par.tʰe.nɔ̌ːn]; Greek: Παρθενώνας, romanised: Parthenónas [parθeˈnonas]) is a former temple on the Athenian Acropolis, Greece, that was dedicated to the goddess Athena. Its decorative sculptures are considered some of the high points of classical Greek art, and the Parthenon is considered an enduring symbol of ancient Greece, Western civilisation, and democracy.

The Parthenon was built in the 5th century BC in thanksgiving for the Greek victory over the Persian invaders during the Greco-Persian Wars. Like most Greek temples, the Parthenon also served as the city treasury. Construction started in 447 BC when the Delian League was at its peak of power. It was completed in 438 BC; work on the artwork and decorations continued until 432 BC. For a time, it served as the treasury of the Delian League, which later became the Athenian Empire.

In the final decade of the 6th century AD, the Parthenon was converted into a Christian church dedicated to the Virgin Mary. After the Ottoman conquest in the mid-15th century, it became a mosque. In the Morean War (1684–1699), a Venetian bomb landed on the Parthenon, which the Ottomans had used as their fortification and defense.

The building's architectural style is considered one of the highest achievements in Greek art and architecture, with its columns and friezes reflecting classical ideals. The sculptures were originally created by sculptors like Phidias, but many have been lost or destroyed over time. The Parthenon was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

The Channel Tunnel is a railway tunnel that connects Folkestone in the United Kingdom with Coquelles in northern France. It was opened in 1994 and remains the only fixed link between Great Britain and the European mainland. The tunnel has an average depth of 45 m below the seabed and runs for 37.9 km (23.5 miles), reaching a depth of 75 m below sea level on average. Although designed for speeds up to 200 km/h, trains are limited to a maximum speed of 160 km/h due to safety concerns.

The tunnel is operated by Eurotunnel and has been used by high-speed passenger trains (Eurostar), road vehicles using LeShuttle services, and freight trains. In 2017, Eurostar trains carried 10.3 million passengers, freight trains transported 1.2 million tonnes of goods, and LeShuttle trains moved around 5,865 containers.

According to Wikipedia, a jet engine is a type of reaction engine that discharges a fast-moving jet of heated gas at high velocity, generating thrust for propulsion. The term typically applies specifically to internal combustion engines such as turbojets, turbofans, ramjets, pulse jets and scramjets which are all air-breathing engines using the Brayton thermodynamic cycle.

The earliest examples were rocket-powered aircraft and waterjet vehicles that flew in the 1920s and 1930s. However, it wasn't until after World War II that the first practical jet engine was developed for military use by Frank Whittle and Hans Peth. 

Early jet engines used turbojets which were relatively inefficient for subsonic flight but became more common as technology improved. In recent decades, a wide variety of types have been developed including high bypass turbofans, ramjets, pulse jets and scramjet engine designs aimed at improving speed and fuel efficiency for aircraft.

Modern jet airliners use these engines to achieve higher speeds and greater efficiency than traditional piston or propeller-powered aeroplanes over long distances. Examples include the Pratt & Whitney JT12A engine used by Boeing 707 and General Electric JT9D engine in McDonnell Douglas DC-8 and other commercial aircraft models from that era onwards, followed by more complex turbofan designs such as the CF6 for Boeing 737 series planes.

Scramjet engines are an advanced air-breathing jet design that use a ram effect on the vehicle's forward motion rather than relying on mechanical compressors. They can theoretically propel vehicles at Mach speeds up to about 4 times their weight and have been tested in experimental designs with promising results for high speed military applications like hypersonic missiles.

In summary, the invention of the jet engine was a significant technological breakthrough that revolutionized aviation by providing greater range, fuel efficiency and operational capabilities compared to traditional piston or propeller-powered aircraft.

Here is the summary of the discovery of oxygen:

The discovery of oxygen was achieved independently by Carl Wilhelm Scheele, Joseph Priestley and Antoine Lavoisier in 1774. They were working separately at nearby chemical laboratories but had similar results in producing a gas called "dephlogisticated air" or "vapour of air." Both men recognized it as an important gas but did not understand its chemical nature until Priestley noted that the color of burning candles was extinguished when they were mixed with "air."

Scheele made oxygen under pressure and at higher temperatures, while Priestley produced oxygen by decomposing hydrogen peroxide. Lavoisier showed that both Scheele's and Priestley's gases combined with combustibles but did not cause combustion itself.

In 1775, Priestley published his work on air in England, making him the first to use the term "oxygen" in its present meaning. This led later chemists to study oxygen gas independently of the other oxygen-producing methods, including Scheele's process for producing it under high pressure and low temperature.

The first commercial extraction was achieved by French chemist Jean-Joseph Groene, whose method used a vacuum chamber with an iron cylinder to extract oxygen from air. This discovery allowed greater use of the element in chemical synthesis until its replacement by synthetic methods came about later on.

To summarize, an airship is a type of aircraft that uses buoyancy to stay airborne. It typically consists of a gasbag filled with lighter-than-air lifting gas, which provides the necessary lift. Early dirigibles used hydrogen as their primary lifting gas due to its high lift-to-weight ratio and ease of availability. However, its flammability led to several fatal accidents.

In contrast, helium is now commonly used as an alternative to hydrogen in airships because it's not flammable but relatively expensive. Rigid airships are made with a frame that holds the envelope in place. Non-rigid and semi-rigid airships can be either gasbags or gas-filled cells within them. The engines, crew quarters, and payload for these aircraft are housed inside gondolas suspended below the lifting envelope.

Rigid airships have steel frames that allow the envelope to stretch without breaking it, while non-rigid models typically use rubberized materials. Rigid airships also have a larger volume capacity than their gas-filled counterparts but can't withstand high temperatures or pressures like those found in extreme weather conditions.

- lookup_6: The Parthenon (; Ancient Greek: Παρθενών, romanised: Parthenōn [par.tʰe.nɔ̌ːn]; Greek: Παρθενώνας, romanised: Parthenónas [parθeˈnonas]) is a former temple on the Athenian Acropolis, Greece, that was dedicated to the goddess Athena. Its decorative sculptures are considered some of the high points of classical Greek art, and the Parthenon is considered an enduring symbol of ancient Greece, Western civilisation, and democracy.

The Parthenon was built in the 5th century BC in thanksgiving for the Greek victory over the Persian invaders during the Greco-Persian Wars. Like most Greek temples, the Parthenon also served as the city treasury. Construction started in 447 BC when the Delian League was at its peak of power. It was completed in 438 BC; work on the artwork and decorations continued until 432 BC. For a time, it served as the treasury of the Delian League, which later became the Athenian Empire.

In the final decade of the 6th century AD, the Parthenon was converted into a Christian church dedicated to the Virgin Mary. After the Ottoman conquest in the mid-15th century, it became a mosque. In the Morean War (1684–1699), a Venetian bomb landed on the Parthenon, which the Ottomans had used as their fortification and defense.

The building's architectural style is considered one of the highest achievements in Greek art and architecture, with its columns and friezes reflecting classical ideals. The sculptures were originally created by sculptors like Phidias, but many have been lost or destroyed over time. The Parthenon was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

- lookup_10: According to Wikipedia, a jet engine is a type of reaction engine that discharges a fast-moving jet of heated gas at high velocity, generating thrust for propulsion. The term typically applies specifically to internal combustion engines such as turbojets, turbofans, ramjets, pulse jets and scramjets which are all air-breathing engines using the Brayton thermodynamic cycle.

The earliest examples were rocket-powered aircraft and waterjet vehicles that flew in the 1920s and 1930s. However, it wasn't until after World War II that the first practical jet engine was developed for military use by Frank Whittle and Hans Peth. 

Early jet engines used turbojets which were relatively inefficient for subsonic flight but became more common as technology improved. In recent decades, a wide variety of types have been developed including high bypass turbofans, ramjets, pulse jets and scramjet engine designs aimed at improving speed and fuel efficiency for aircraft.

Modern jet airliners use these engines to achieve higher speeds and greater efficiency than traditional piston or propeller-powered aeroplanes over long distances. Examples include the Pratt & Whitney JT12A engine used by Boeing 707 and General Electric JT9D engine in McDonnell Douglas DC-8 and other commercial aircraft models from that era onwards, followed by more complex turbofan designs such as the CF6 for Boeing 737 series planes.

Scramjet engines are an advanced air-breathing jet design that use a ram effect on the vehicle's forward motion rather than relying on mechanical compressors. They can theoretically propel vehicles at Mach speeds up to about 4 times their weight and have been tested in experimental designs with promising results for high speed military applications like hypersonic missiles.

In summary, the invention of the jet engine was a significant technological breakthrough that revolutionized aviation by providing greater range, fuel efficiency and operational capabilities compared to traditional piston or propeller-powered aircraft.

Rigid airships also have a larger volume capacity than their gas-filled counterparts but can't withstand high temperatures or pressures like those found in extreme weather conditions.
